title: Knowing becoming and destruction together
theme: Whoever knows sambhūti and vināśa together crosses death by the one and attains the deathless by the other.

words.context: Śaṅkara reads it as a-sambhūti, ‘non-becoming’, the unmanifest, by an elided a- («इत्यत्रावर्णलोपेन निर्देशो द्रष्टव्यः»)

words.role: links sambhūtim and vināśam (ca … ca, ‘both … and’)

words.context: Śaṅkara: what has destruction as its property, the product, Hiraṇyagarbha

words.role: subject of veda; correlative of the understood subject of aśnute
sums up the pair, in apposition to ubhayam

words.gram: verb, root vid (2nd class, P.), perfect 3rd sg. with present sense

words.context: Śaṅkara, on the parallel mantra 11, takes ‘together’ as ‘to be practised by one and the same person’
Śaṅkara: «अधर्मकामादिदोषजातं च मृत्युं» — together with lack of power (anaiśvarya), the unrighteousness, desire and other faults

words.role: prior action of the subject of aśnute

words.context: Śaṅkara: «असम्भूत्या अव्याकृतोपासनया», ‘by non-becoming, the worship of the unmanifest’
Śaṅkara: «अमृतं प्रकृतिलयलक्षणम्», immortality in the sense of dissolution into prakṛti

words.gram: verb, root aś (5th class, Ā.), present 3rd sg.

sandhi.rule: P. 8.3.23 (मोऽनुस्वारः), written ं before c (or as the class nasal ñ).
yaḥ + tat: visarga before t becomes s (P. 8.3.34 (विसर्जनीयस्य सः)); tat + veda: t voiced to d; veda + ubhayam: a + u → o (P. 6.1.87 (आद्गुणः)).
ā + a → ā (P. 6.1.101 (अकः सवर्णे दीर्घः)); a final m before a vowel is kept. Madhva’s text marks the elided a with an avagraha (सम्भूत्याऽमृतम्).

Written as it is, the junction is tīrtvā + sambhūtyā. But tīrtvā + asambhūtyā would give the same letters, ā + a → ā (P. 6.1.101 (अकः सवर्णे दीर्घः)), distinguished only by an avagraha that the witnesses do not write. Śaṅkara’s reading asambhūtyā is therefore possible in the second line without changing a letter; in the first line, where sambhūtiṃ begins the verse, it is not.

morphology.note: sam + √bhū with the action-noun suffix -ti (P. 3.3.94 (स्त्रियां क्तिन्)). The Mādhyandina pada-pāṭha divides «सम्भू॑ति॒मिति॒ सम्ऽभू॑तिम्», not asambhūtim; Śaṅkara’s a- is an interpretive restoration, which he justifies by the result the Upaniṣad assigns: «‘सम्भूतिं च विनाशं च’ इत्यत्रावर्णलोपेन निर्देशो द्रष्टव्यः, प्रकृतिलयफलश्रुत्यनुरोधात्».

vi + √naś, ‘to perish’, with the suffix -a: ‘perishing’. Śaṅkara takes it of the thing that has perishing as its property, by identifying the property with its bearer: «विनाशो धर्मो यस्य कार्यस्य स तेन धर्मिणा अभेदेनोच्यते ‘विनाशः’ इति». Mahīdhara, in his first explanation, derives vināśa ‘having destruction’ with the possessive suffix ac of the arśa-ādi group («अर्शआदित्वादच्प्रत्ययः», cf. P. 5.2.127 (अर्शआदिभ्योऽच्)) and applies it to the perishable body.

In Mahīdhara’s second explanation the a- is restored here instead: «अत्र विनाशशब्दद्वये अवर्णलोपो द्रष्टव्यः पृषोदरादित्वात्» — ‘in both occurrences of vināśa an elided a is to be understood, as an irregular form’. He appeals to the class of forms accepted as taught, P. 6.3.109 (पृषोदरादीनि यथोपदिष्टम्). The pada-pāṭha gives «विना॒शेनेति॑ विना॒शेन॑» and «वि॒ना॒शमिति॑ विऽना॒शम्».
Perfect of √vid used with present meaning (‘knows’), a regular feature of this root.

Absolutive of √tṝ, ‘to cross’: an action prior to the main verb with the same agent (P. 3.4.21 (समानकर्तृकयोः पूर्वकाले)). Deśika, commenting on mantra 12, rejects taking tṝ in these verses in the sense of ‘attaining’, as he had for the parallel mantra 11.
√aś, 5th class ātmanepada, ‘to reach, attain’ (distinct from aś, 9th class, ‘to eat’).

anvaya: यः सम्भूतिम् च विनाशम् च तत् उभयम् सह वेद [सः] विनाशेन मृत्युम् तीर्त्वा सम्भूत्या अमृतम् अश्नुते ।
syntax: A relative sentence (yaḥ … veda) and its main clause (the subject sa is understood). The objects of veda are sambhūtim and vināśam, linked by ca … ca and summed up by tad ubhayam, ‘that, both’; saha, ‘together’, says how they are known. The main clause takes the two objects up again in the instrumental and gives each a result: by vināśa one crosses death (absolutive tīrtvā), by sambhūti one attains the deathless (aśnute). The order of the pair is reversed in the second line (sambhūti first, then vināśa; then vināśa first, then sambhūti), a chiasmus that mantra 11 has in the same way with vidyā and avidyā.

ambiguities.topic: sambhūti or asambhūti in this mantra
ambiguities.note: The text has sambhūtim and sambhūtyā. Śaṅkara reads both as asambhūti (the unmanifest), because vināśa already stands for the manifest Hiraṇyagarbha and because mantra 13, as he reads it, assigns dissolution into prakṛti to asambhava. Mahīdhara, in his second explanation, keeps sambhūti and restores the a- in vināśa instead (avināśa, the unmanifest). Deśika, Madhva and Mahīdhara’s first explanation restore nothing. The pada-pāṭha supports the text as it stands.

ambiguities.topic: What is ‘death’ and what is ‘the deathless’?
ambiguities.note: For Śaṅkara, death is lack of power and the faults of desire, and ‘immortality’ only dissolution into prakṛti, relative and not liberation. For Mahīdhara’s first explanation, death is crossed by desireless works done with the perishable body, and immortality is liberation («मुक्तिं प्राप्नोति»). For Deśika, crossing death is removing the obstacles, and immortality the attainment of Brahman.
Madhva’s mūla as keyed lacks the second ca (सम्भूतिं च विनाशं यस्तद्), which leaves the half-line one syllable short; corrections.json classifies it for review against a printed text.

metre.name: anuṣṭubh
metre.note: Two half-lines of 16 syllables. Madhva’s keyed text, without the second च, would have 15 in the first.

translation.literal: Whoever knows becoming (sambhūti) and destruction (vināśa) — that, both together — having crossed death by destruction, attains the deathless by becoming.
translation.readable: Whoever knows both together — becoming and perishing — crosses death through the one that perishes and reaches the deathless through becoming.

beginner: This verse resolves the riddle of the last two. There, two one-sided paths each led into darkness. Here, someone who knows both together — what comes into being and what passes away — crosses over death by means of the one and reaches the deathless by means of the other. Notice that the verse does not ask you to choose. Coming into being and passing away are not rivals; they belong to the same life, the way breathing in and breathing out belong to one breath. Teachers disagree, sometimes sharply, about what exactly the two words point to — parts of the universe, stages of a spiritual path, or powers of God — and one great teacher even reads a hidden ‘not’ into the verse. But on its surface the lesson is about wholeness: understanding comes from holding together what we usually separate.
analogy: A gardener who understands both how seeds sprout and how plants die back works with the whole cycle of the year, instead of being surprised by each season.

commentary.q: What does the mantra itself state?
commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: It describes one who ‘knows both together’ — sambhūti and vināśa — and says what that person achieves: by vināśa, the crossing of death; by sambhūti, the attainment of the deathless. The pair here is sambhūti and vināśa, not sambhūti and asambhūti as in mantra 12. The form copies mantra 11 (vidyā and avidyā) exactly. The text does not say whether the deathless here is final liberation or a lesser immortality.

commentary.q: Why does Śaṅkara read a hidden ‘a-’?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: In Śaṅkara’s reading mantra 12 opposed asambhūti (prakṛti) and sambhūti (Hiraṇyagarbha), and mantra 13 gave dissolution into prakṛti as the fruit of asambhava. Mantra 14 names vināśa, which he takes as Hiraṇyagarbha — what has destruction as its property. If vināśa is Hiraṇyagarbha, the other member of the pair must be the unmanifest; hence his note: «‘सम्भूतिं च विनाशं च’ इत्यत्रावर्णलोपेन निर्देशो द्रष्टव्यः, प्रकृतिलयफलश्रुत्यनुरोधात्». By the worship of Hiraṇyagarbha one gains powers and crosses ‘death’ — lack of power and the faults of desire — and by the worship of the unmanifest one attains an ‘immortality’ that is dissolution into prakṛti («असम्भूत्या अव्याकृतोपासनया अमृतं प्रकृतिलयलक्षणम् अश्नुते»). The combination of the two worships is fitting because both serve one human aim («समुच्चयः सम्भूत्यसम्भूत्युपासनयोर्युक्तः»).

commentary.q: How do Deśika and Mahīdhara read the pair without Śaṅkara’s restoration?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Deśika: by vināśa, contemplated, one removes the obstacle; by sambhūti, contemplated, one attains Brahman («अनुसन्धीयमानेन विनाशेन प्रतिबन्धमपोह्य, सम्भूत्याऽनुसन्धीयमानया ब्रह्म प्राप्नोति»). He offers a second sense of vināśa: the destruction of pride and hypocrisy, of violence and theft, and of the outward-turned senses. He holds that reading the words as creation and dissolution gives not ‘even a trace of fitness’ for the division of results («सृष्टिप्रलयादिविवक्षया मृत्युतरणामृतप्राप्तिरूपफलविभागवचनस्यौचित्यलवोऽपि नोपलभ्यते»). Mahīdhara’s first explanation takes sambhūti as the supreme Brahman, the cause of the world’s origin («सर्वजगत्संभवैकहेतुं परं ब्रह्म»), and vināśa as the perishable body: knowing embodied self and body together, one does desireless works with the body, purifies the mind, and by self-knowledge attains liberation.

commentary.q: What does the received text allow?
commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: In the second half-line the restoration costs nothing: tīrtvā + asambhūtyā and tīrtvā + sambhūtyā are written with the same letters, since ā + a gives ā. In the first half-line sambhūtiṃ opens the verse and no sandhi could have swallowed an a-; there the restoration is an interpretive device, not a choice between readings of the same letters. The Mādhyandina pada-pāṭha (VS 40.11) analyses the words as sam-bhūtim, vi-nāśam, sam-bhūtyā, without a negative. Mahīdhara’s alternative — the a- in vināśa — shows that the tradition itself was not agreed on where the elision lies.

commentary.q: How is this mantra related to mantra 11?
commentary.label: comparative
commentary.text: Mantras 11 and 14 have one template: ‘whoever knows X and Y together, crossing death by Y, attains the deathless by X’. In 11 the pair is vidyā and avidyā; in 14 sambhūti and vināśa. Śaṅkara reads both as combinations within the realm of meditation and ritual, short of liberation; Deśika reads both as stages of the one path to Brahman. The parallelism is the strongest evidence that the two triads were meant to be read together, whatever their terms denote.

advaita.text: sambhūti is to be read asambhūti, the unmanifest cause, and vināśa is Hiraṇyagarbha. Worship of Hiraṇyagarbha yields powers («हिरण्यगर्भोपासनेन ह्यणिमादिप्राप्तिः फलम्») and crosses ‘death’; worship of the unmanifest yields dissolution into prakṛti. The ‘immortality’ is relative; liberation is by knowledge of the Self alone, as mantras 6–8 teach.

visistadvaita.text: The two contemplations are limbs of the knowledge of Brahman: destruction of the obstacles (or of pride, violence and outward-turned senses) and the experience of Brahman. By the first one crosses death, by the second one attains Brahman («सम्भूत्याऽनुसन्धीयमानया ब्रह्म प्राप्नोति»). No a- is restored and the cosmic reading is rejected.

dvaita.ref: Īśāvāsyopaniṣad-bhāṣya on mantras 12–14 (incomplete in the digital text)
dvaita.text: In the verse Madhva cites, one who knows the Lord as both the creator and the destroyer is freed from the bondage of the body by the knowledge of his destroying («यो वेद संहृतिज्ञानाद्देहबन्धाद्विमुच्यते»), and by knowing him as the agent of bliss, knowledge and the rest reaches their manifestation. Knowing the Lord’s supremacy, distinct even from the released, one is liberated («ततो विष्णोः परोत्कर्षं सम्यग्ज्ञात्वा विमुच्यते»).

schools.disagreement: The schools divide on three points: whether the text is to be read as it stands (Deśika, Madhva, Mahīdhara’s first explanation) or with a restored a- (Śaṅkara in sambhūti, Mahīdhara’s second explanation in vināśa); whether the terms denote cosmic principles (Śaṅkara), stages of the path (Deśika) or the Lord’s powers (Madhva); and whether the ‘immortality’ attained is relative (Śaṅkara) or liberation (Deśika, Madhva, Mahīdhara’s first explanation).

parallels.note: ‘At the coming of night they dissolve into that same thing called the unmanifest.’ A thematic association with Śaṅkara’s prakṛtilaya, dissolution into the unmanifest; not a reference to this mantra.

‘Shaking off the body, I, my self made, [attain] the unmade Brahma-world.’ Deśika cites this passage (with abhisambhavāni) for sambhūti as the attainment of Brahman; the Advaita Sharada text reads abhisambhavāmi.

contemporary.text: Most people live as though growth were the whole story and decline an interruption. The mantra puts coming-into-being and perishing side by side and says that knowing them together is what carries one past death. Without claiming that this is what the commentators meant, a modern reader may hear in it something about aging: that a life understood only as accumulation is incomplete, and that coming to terms with what passes may be part of reaching what does not. This is a reflection, separate from the exegesis above.

reflect.beginner: Think of something in your life that began and something that ended this year. How are the two connected?
reflect.deeper: Can perishing itself be a means — something by which one ‘crosses death’ — and if so, what is it that perishes?
reflect.practice: At the end of each day for a week, note one thing that came into being and one that came to an end. On the last day, read the list and look for the pattern.

references.text: The pada-pāṭha printed with the Mādhyandina witness (VS 40.11) analyses «सम्भू॑ति॒मिति॒ सम्ऽभू॑तिम्», «वि॒ना॒शमिति॑ विऽना॒शम्» and «सम्भू॒त्येति॒ सम्ऽभू॑त्या».

flags.note: Śaṅkara’s and Mahīdhara’s restored a- are reported, not adopted: the literal translation follows the letters and the pada-pāṭha.
Madhva’s mūla as keyed lacks the second च (corrections.json, class review), and his comment on 12–14 survives only in part in the digital source.
